articles.title: Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences
articles.summary: The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.
body: Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “ convinced ” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.
points: The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company.

articles.title: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
articles.summary: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content.
body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets.

So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base.
points: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a different kind of GTA — so it needed a different kind of ending
articles.summary: In most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll. It could be Los Santos or a twisted take on Manhattan, but the idea is that the main story is just one part of the experience.
body: GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

“In this one it didn’t make sense,” Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North, told me ahead of the game’s launch. “Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”
This story contains light spoilers for the ending of Grand Theft Auto VI, along with a key plot point from chapter 1.

To be clear, you can still play GTA VI after the main storyline wraps up. But in order for that to happen, you have to zip back in time to a moment before a pivotal decision — I won’t spoil it for you — that alters the lives of main characters Jason and Lucia, along with their young son Tomás, who they’re attempting to get custody of. Nelson says the team tried “all sorts of things” but soon realized that “in no way did it make sense” to have the game end like a traditional GTA experience.

articles.title: Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture
articles.summary: In church basements and warehouses, Americans are building cozy yet radical spaces to encourage each other to fix broken items instead of throwing them away.
body: This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”
points: In church basements and warehouses, Americans are building cozy yet radical spaces to encourage each other to fix broken items instead of throwing them away.

articles.title: The British Government is Turning Everyone Into a Prepper
articles.summary: Forget guns and underground bunkers. Britain’s burgeoning survivalist movement is more worried about backup power, baby formula, and making friends with the neighbors.
body: In 2010, the UK experienced one of its coldest ever winters, with heavy snowfall bringing major roads to a standstill. Brian, an engineer in central Scotland, had little food in the house. He donned a backpack, took one of his children’s sledges, and trudged a mile and half to queue outside the nearest supermarket. Shelves were emptying, and tempers were fraying.

Next time, Brian decided, he would be prepared. “It’s very hard to look your kids in the eye when you’re looking at a relatively empty cupboard,” he says. Brian started building up a store of non-perishable food and other supplies, ready for unexpected shortages. He’s now part of the UK’s prepper community—a group of survivalists who plan proactively for emergency situations such as natural disasters or infrastructure breakdowns. He shares his tips on YouTube as Scottishprepper73; he reckons his family could live a full year off his stash.
points: Britain’s burgeoning survivalist movement is more worried about backup power, baby formula, and making friends with the neighbors.
